Q_EC.text: I actually brought it up myself, which I think was the right call, and my manager was genuinely receptive -- she thanked me for being open and said right away that she wanted to make sure I had what I needed. we ended up talking for about an hour (longer than I planned, honestly) and then she looped in HR, not in a heavy formal way but just to document the accommodations properly so there'd be no ambiguity later on. What we landed on was a flexible start time for mornings when my anxiety is particularly bad, the option to work from home when I need to decompress, and a standing check-in every two weeks that I can cancel if things are going well. I was genuinely surprised by how low-key they made it feel, and I think that's the kind of thing that encourages other people to disclose too -- when it's treated as a practical conversation rather than a crisis it removes so much of the stigma around asking for help in the first place

Q_CC.text: a few close colleagues already knew, so those conversations were pretty low-key -- more like "hey I wanted to be upfront about this" and them saying something along the lines of "thanks for telling me, that makes sense actually." one coworker mentioned she'd been dealing with something similar for years and hadn't told anyone, and I think that exchange kind of meant a lot to both of us, like it opened something up that hadn't been open before. nobody made it weird or awkward, which honestly I was half-expecting at least from someone, but it just didn't happen that way.

Q_CW.text: it was actually the same coworker I mentioned -- she came to me a few days after my own disclosure, which felt like maybe that's what gave her the opening, and she talked about having anxiety too, pretty severe at points, and how she'd been managing it quietly for a long time without telling anyone at work. she was a bit tearful, not in a distressing way but more like relief, I think, and I mostly just listened and told her I thought it took a lot to say it out loud. we ended up having a longer conversation about whether it was worth talking to her manager the way I had, and I shared what that process looked like for me, not to push her but just so she'd know it was an option that didn't have to be scary.

Q_PE.text: at my previous job I did bring it up once, though it was a less smooth conversation -- my manager at the time was sympathetic but clearly a bit uncomfortable with it, like he didn't quite know what to do with the information, and what came out of it was basically just "let us know if you need anything" without any real structure around it. nothing bad happened but it also didn't go anywhere, which I think is actually how a lot of these conversations end and why having a more proactive process matters

Q_PC.text: at my previous job I was a bit more guarded with coworkers than I am now, partly because the culture felt less explicitly supportive and I wasn't sure how it would land, so I only really told one person -- a teammate I was genuinely close to -- and she was kind about it, said something like "I wondered if something was going on, I'm glad you told me." but it kind of stopped there, she wasn't sure what to do with it any more than my manager was, and I think that's just the texture of workplaces that don't have any real infrastructure around this stuff, everyone means well but nobody quite knows their role. I didn't tell anyone else there, which in retrospect I think was the right call for that environment even if it meant carrying more of it quietly than I do now -- it's one of the reasons I was so deliberate about finding somewhere different.

Q_CA.text: honestly, less negatively than I expected, and I think part of that is because I've been fairly intentional about where and when I disclose -- at my current job it's actually been a net positive in some ways, in that my manager knows what I need and I'm not burning energy pretending everything is fine all the time, which lets me do better work. there was a period at my previous job where I did quietly wonder if being open had made me seem less reliable in some people's eyes, nothing concrete ever happened but the feeling was there, and I think that ambient uncertainty is its own kind of cost even when there are no visible consequences. so I wouldn't say it's derailed anything, but I also don't think I've been naive about the fact that it carries some risk depending on the environment -- which is part of why I think the structural stuff, like having actual accommodations documented and a manager who's explicitly on board, matters so much. it changes the calculation from "is this safe" to "I know it's safe"

Q_BH.text: the circumstance was at my previous job -- I brought it up during a regular one-on-one with my manager, not dramatically, just as context for why I sometimes needed a bit more flexibility, and his response was kind in tone but essentially landed nowhere. he said the right things in the moment ("thank you for sharing that," "we want to support you") but then nothing actually followed from it, no accommodation was discussed, no follow-up was scheduled, nothing was documented, and when I came back a few weeks later to ask about it he seemed a bit caught off guard, like he hadn't really held onto the conversation. what made it badly handled wasn't hostility at all -- it was more the complete absence of any process, like disclosure was something that happened and then was over rather than something that was supposed to open a door to actual support. and I think what took me longest to shake was that ambient uncertainty I mentioned about whether I'd now been quietly categorized as someone less reliable, even though nothing was ever said or done explicitly -- nobody was unkind, nobody penalized me for anything, but the not-knowing has its own weight and I think that's actually the most common form of bad handling, the well-meaning shrug that leaves you with no idea where you stand.

Q_SH.text: the current job is basically the whole story here, and I think what made it well-handled was the combination of attitude and actual follow-through, because you can have one without the other and it doesn't really work. my manager's initial reaction was warm and unhesitating -- she didn't get awkward or start hedging about what she could and couldn't do, she just said "okay, what would actually help you" which is such a disarmingly simple question and yet I'd never been asked it that directly before. and then the things we agreed on (the flexible start time, the WFH days when I need them, the fortnightly check-in) actually got documented properly through HR, not in a punitive or surveillance-y way but just so there was something concrete that we both understood -- I think the documentation piece is underrated, because it means neither of us has to hold the whole thing informally in our heads and wonder if the other person still remembers what we agreed to. the other thing that made it genuinely good was that my manager framed it as ongoing rather than a one-time conversation, like she'd checked in a few times since then just to see how things were going, not in a way that felt like monitoring but in the way you'd check in on any colleague who'd told you something real about themselves. that continuity is what made it feel like support rather than just a good moment that then dissolved.

Q_ID.text: honestly the biggest gap I see is that most companies treat mental health as a reactive thing -- something that only gets addressed once someone's already struggling and visible about it, rather than building the infrastructure ahead of time so disclosure isn't the only way in. training managers to actually respond rather than just acknowledge is probably the most high-leverage thing, because in my experience the well-meaning shrug is way more common than any kind of explicit hostility and it does real damage even when nobody intends it. documented accommodation processes help too, because if people dont know the ask is even an option they won't make it, and if there's no process then the outcome depends entirely on who your manager happens to be that week. and I think normalization at the cultural level -- leadership actually talking about this stuff openly, not in a performative campaign way but as an ongoing thing -- changes the baseline calculation people are making when they decide whether it's safe to say something.

I can take "anxiety days" when I need to. I do take them unpaid since that gives me less anxiety and then it doesn't show on the budget higher up (A large company has a small office in my country and these are all arrangements at that office.) but he is fine with me taking them as paid sick days, again my choice not to do so. All I have to do is inform my team when I'm showing up very late or not at all or working from home, it is such a relief to be able to have honest open communication and has lessened a lot of anxiety that I had about "being sick a lot" or if they thought I was a lazy person. My anxiety also affects my sleep a lot and now since making these adjustments I have not had to show up for work unslept and the even though I have fewer hours some weeks then I did before they are more productive and I'm happier about them. He did ask a lot about if there was anything at work that was making things worse and what they could do better, and when they were changing up teams at my office I was asked before anything was finalized.

Q_PC.text: Given the previous employer context, I kept things to myself there too — no disclosure, no conversation worth describing.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, in my current role it hasn't been negative at all — if anything, it's positioned me as someone colleagues feel safe approaching. My previous employer is where I'd have worried about it, but I never disclosed there so the question didn't arise.

Q_EC.text: i told my manager i was dealing with depression and that i'd just come out of treatment for alcoholism. he seemed supportive at first -- said all the right things about "working with me" and keeping it between us. then about three weeks later he brought it up in a performance review as evidence i was unreliable. no support was ever actually put in place, my disclosure just got weaponized

Q_CC.text: a few coworkers already knew about the alcoholism because we'd gotten close outside of work. when i opened up about struggling again they didn't flinch -- one of them checked in with me almost every morning for a couple months, another would just text asking if i wanted to grab lunch. honestly those friendships kept me functional in a way no formal support ever did

Q_CW.text: one of the people i mentioned -- the one who texted about lunch -- came to me maybe a year in and said she was really struggling with anxiety, bad enough it was affecting her sleep and her ability to focus at work. she wasn't looking for solutions, just needed to say it out loud to someone she trusted. i listened, checked in when i could. felt like the least i could do after what she'd done for me.

Q_PE.text: didn't go nearly as well as i hoped. i was still pretty early in figuring out the depression piece -- hadn't addressed the drinking yet -- and i mentioned to my supervisor that i was having a hard time. she sort of nodded and said to "reach out to HR if i needed resources." that was it. no follow-up, nothing changed. i don't think she knew what to do, but the silence felt like a door shutting

Q_PC.text: at that job i didn't really open up to coworkers the way i later did. i was still in denial about a lot of it, honestly. one or two people noticed i seemed off and asked if i was okay -- i gave the standard "just tired" answer and they let it go. i think if i'd been more honest they might have responded better, but i wasn't ready and the environment didn't exactly invite it

Q_CA.text: the performance review thing set me back pretty concretely -- i got passed over for a project lead role about six months after that, and i'm fairly certain it was connected. hard to prove, but the timing and what my manager said made it obvious. i've been more careful since about what i disclose and to who, which honestly feels like its own kind of loss

Q_BH.text: the performance review is the one that really sticks. i'd disclosed voluntarily, in good faith, because i thought my manager was trustworthy -- he'd been warm about it, said the right things. then three weeks later i'm sitting in a formal review with HR in the room and he's citing my depression and recovery as evidence of "inconsistency." there was nothing i could say that didn't sound defensive. i felt exposed and honestly a little stupid for trusting him

Q_SH.text: the coworker stuff i already mentioned -- that was the well-handled version, honestly. no official process, no HR involved, just people who actually knew me and showed up. the morning check-ins, the lunch texts. it didn't fix anything structural but it kept me tethered. what made it work was that nobody made it weird or treated me like i was suddenly fragile. they just kept being my friends

Q_ID.text: the biggest thing would be actual confidentiality protections -- legal ones, with real teeth for managers who weaponize disclosures in reviews. beyond that, i think companies overinvest in EAP programs nobody uses and underinvest in just letting people be actual humans with each other. the peer support that helped me wasn't a program, it was people. culture has to come first or none of the formal stuff matters

Q_AE.text: just that the peer thing can't be faked. you can't program it into a policy

Q_CC.text: one coworker in particular, we kind of mutually disclosed to each other over time. she deals with anxiety, I have depression and ADHD, so we just... talk about it pretty openly. it's been helpful honestly, having someone at work who gets it without you having to explain everything from scratch.

Q_CW.text: we check in on each other pretty regularly. she brought it up kind of gradually -- mentioned she was struggling with anxiety, we just started talking from there. it wasn't like a big formal conversation, more just something that developed naturally over time.

Q_PE.text: previous job was a different story. I wasn't as open about it — didn't really trust the environment tbh. I did eventually tell my manager about the ADHD just because it was affecting my work in obvious ways, and she was... fine about it, I guess. not dismissive, but no real support either. kind of just acknowledged it and moved on.

Q_PC.text: didn't really disclose to anyone there. the culture felt pretty closed off so I just kept it to myself.

Q_CA.text: honestly, not as much as I feared. the current job has been fine -- I think being upfront about it early on helped set expectations. but I do wonder sometimes if it's shaped how people see me, even when things are going well.

Q_BH.text: previous job, when I told my manager about the ADHD. she just kind of nodded and said "okay, let me know if you need anything" and that was it. no follow-up, nothing changed. I didn't even know what to ask for at that point, and she didn't offer anything so it just... got dropped.

Q_SH.text: current job, my manager actually followed up after I told her. checked in a couple weeks later to see how things were going. it wasnt a big deal made of it, just... she remembered, which meant a lot honestly.

Q_ID.text: normalize the conversation earlier, not just when someone is already struggling. like, if managers were actually trained to bring it up proactively -- not in a weird way, just making it clear it's okay to talk about -- I think a lot of people wouldnt wait until things were bad. and actual follow-up matters. saying "let me know if you need anything" and never mentioning it again isn't support, it's just... covering yourself.

Q_AE.text: just that the medication side of things doesn't really get asked about, and it's kind of a big part of managing this stuff day to day. like whether it's okay to tell your employer you're on medication, what that might mean for how they see you. that's something I've thought about a lot.

Q_EC.text: Told my manager I had anxiety and depression, pretty casually tbh. She nodded, said "thanks for letting me know" and that was kind of it. There were bigger fires going on at the time -- the whole team was in chaos -- so it didnt really go anywhere after that.

Q_CC.text: Mentioned it offhandedly to a couple of colleagues, same thing -- anxiety, depression, no big deal. they were sympathetic I suppose, one said she dealt with something similar. But honestly the office was such a mess at the time that it kind of got absorbed into everything else going on.

Q_CW.text: They mentioned burnout mostly, said they were really struggling to keep up. I just listened, said I got it. nothing dramatic, it was just one of those hallway conversations that happens when everyones already at their limit.

Q_PE.text: Similar thing, told them about the anxiety upfront when things started getting bad. My manager at the time kind of just shrugged and said "okay, let us know if you need anything" -- and that was it, nothing actually came of it.

Q_PC.text: Pretty similar to now honestly -- mentioned it to a few people, got a "oh yeah me too" or "that sucks, hope things get better." nobody really made it a thing which I suppose was fine. the office dysfunction kind of drowned everything out anyway.

Q_CA.text: Honestly not much, or at least nothing I could point to directly. I suppose theres always that low-level worry in the back of your head, but the workplaces I've been in were already so dysfunctional that mental health stuff was pretty far down the list of reasons things went sideways.

Q_BH.text: It wasn't dramatic or anything. I said I was struggling and my manager basically just went "yeah okay" and moved on. No follow-up, no check-in, nothing referred to HR. I suppose the threshold for unsupportive is higher when the whole place is already on fire -- but still, it would've been nice if someone actually did something.

Q_SH.text: There was one colleague, different job, who actually followed up a few days later to check in. Nothing formal, just a "hey how are you doing" over Slack. I suppose that's a low bar but it genuinely meant something at the time -- someone actually remembered.

Q_ID.text: Actual follow-through would help -- not just an EAP link in the onboarding doc that nobody uses. I suppose the basic thing is managers who actually check in, not as policy but as like, a normal thing. the industry talks a good game but most places are too chaotic to act on any of it.
